B.C. unions demand political leaders bring ferry building home after a bruising offshore contract backlash.
Evidence: Union coalition report, party platform commitments, BC Ferries offshore deal
#BCPoli #Labour #Shipbuilding

All major B.C. political parties have committed to insourcing future ferry construction and rebuilding local maritime industrial capacity.
Stated Judgement: (+1.00, +1.00) — Greater Good

Decades of underinvestment and high costs pushed BC Ferries to China; campaign promises face severe infrastructure and funding hurdles.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.42, -0.38) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — Fall into Destruction.

Integrity: Conditionally Sound (Hypocrisy: 1.82, z: 2)
Unions and the Centre for Future Work released a report showing local ferry builds could generate $1.5 billion in GDP and thousands of jobs.
Following public backlash over BC Ferries hiring a Chinese shipyard for four new vessels, all three B.C. political parties pledged domestic builds.

The Bright Side:
All political parties now acknowledge the strategic necessity of local shipbuilding and manufacturing capacity.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing political campaign rhetoric (WHAT parties promise) with actual industrial and drydock capacity (WHERE ships can be built).

Social Physics Analysis:
The political parties operated under a smart selfish loop, outsourcing to cut short-term costs until public backlash forced a pivot toward protectionist pretexts. Unions are pushing for structural empowerment, demanding that government investment match rhetoric to achieve real industrial renewal.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
When political convenience collides with structural neglect, the path requires moving from hollow campaign promises toward genuine capital investment. (can be -> May be)

The Unavoidable Truth: Local shipbuilding requires billions in sustained government investment and upgraded drydock infrastructure.

The Unavoidable Lie: Politicians claim a simple executive order can instantly replace lost domestic industrial capacity.

Alethekanon:
Campaign pledges cannot magically summon shipyards without long-term capital commitment and infrastructure development.

Awwthekanon:
It hurts to see our skilled trades pushed overseas while local workers stand ready to build with pride and care.

Brothekanon:
Turns out outsourcing ferries to save a buck comes back to haunt politicians when voters realize the yards are empty.

"If a country is governed with tolerance, the people are comfortable." [Tao Te Ching 60] PASS (Harmonic Vector)
Lasting prosperity requires aligning public policy with real productive capacity rather than empty rhetoric.

Our model is simple: if more of our readers sign up to support The Tyee, we can keep up with rising costs and keep adding more talented journalists to our roster and set them loose on uncovering truths that would otherwise not see the light of day.

Please help us prove that independent journalism thrives with reader support.

After a year of political discontent over BC Ferries’ decision to hire a Chinese state-owned shipyard to build four new vessels, the three front-runners in the B.C. election have all committed to supporting ferry-building in this province.

One lucky Tyee reader will receive a family pack of tickets to The Cultch’s annual holiday production, plus a gift card to Bombay Kitchen.

Construction unions have been urging the B.C. government for months to ensure BC Ferries vessels are built in this province.

“This is not a partisan issue for us,” said Brynn Bourke, executive director of the BC Building Trades. “This is about what makes sense for British Columbia, about creating B.C.  jobs, and about rebuilding this industry.”

The BC Building Trades, which represents about 45,000 unionized construction workers in 19 local craft unions, was one of 17 organizations that called on the B.C. government to build ferries in this province ahead of the election.

And while not all the top parties have announced ferry construction plans, the Conservative Party of BC, the BC Green Party and the incumbent BC NDP have all included commitments to insource more ferry construction in their platforms.

Seaspan, the largest shipyard in the Vancouver area, said it welcomed efforts to expand local shipbuilding. Meanwhile, BC Ferries spokesperson Kit Billings said the company would hold off on commenting until after the election.

“We don't want to speculate on potential future government policies,” Billings said in an email. “I appreciate this doesn't directly answer your questions, but once a new government is formed and any new policies are established, we're happy to discuss what they mean for BC Ferries.”

Due in part to high labour costs and a lack of dry-dock space in Canada, foreign shipyards can often build vessels cheaper than Canadian firms can.

That’s why, when BC Ferries first announced plans to build four new vessels, Seaspan turned down the call.

“As BC Ferries has outlined… cost is a primary issue and therefore, no bidder will be incentivized to include significant Canadian/BC domestic content in their bids,” Seaspan said in a press release at the time.

“Canadian shipyards and their supply chains cannot compete with low wage countries that have lower employment standards, lower environmental standards and lower safety standards than Canada and B.C.”

Nearly a year later in June 2025, BC Ferries announced it would hire China Merchants Industry Weihai Shipyards to build the new ferries. The announcement brought backlash from across the political spectrum.

Then-Conservative Party of BC leader John Rustad said the decision contradicts the government’s own promises. Mike Farnworth, who was B.C.’s transportation minister at the time, also said he was unhappy with the decision. Even former federal transport minister Chrystia Freeland publicly said she was dismayed by the deal.

At the end of August, a union-led initiative called “Build Them Here” called on the government to help B.C. shipyards make competitive shipbuilding bids.

The coalition of unions partnered with the Centre for Future Work on a report that estimated building the new ferries in B.C. would have generated $1.5 billion in additional GDP in Canada and  returned $400 million in revenue to the government.

The report also found building the four ferries in B.C. would create 10,000 “person-years” of work. That’s a term used by economists to measure the amount of work done by one person throughout an entire year.  In reality, Bourke said it would translate to thousands of shipbuilding jobs.

According to Bourke, with the BC Building Trades, the primary hurdles affecting local shipyards include government investment and the amount of drydock space available to start building ships in B.C.

Bourke said the coalition had several policy recommendations that include requiring BC Ferries to build in B.C., launching a task force aimed at expanding the province’s shipbuilding capacity and directing BC Ferries to release a vessel replacement schedule that would help companies plan for demand.

“Canadian Shipyards have said they didn't feel they could competitively bid, and so they did not bid,” Bourke said.

“If we continue to repeat the conditions that led to awarding this contract to China, and we do everything the exact same way as during the last call, then we will continue to offshore work.”

In the week before calling a snap election, Premier David Eby told the Union of BC Municipalities that he would direct BC Ferries to ensure its next vessels are built in the province.

On the campaign trail, Eby also committed to working with the federal government to build  a new B.C. shipyard, to build both B.C. ferries and contribute to national defence projects. (Since 2010, the federal government has been investing in the National Shipbuilding Strategy to make up for years of inactivity and lost capacity in domestic shipbuilding.)

In an Oct. 13 press release, the NDP said B.C. had up to $250 million available that it might put toward the project through the Strategic Investment Fund, a fund it uses to invest in the private sector.

Meanwhile, the Conservative Party of BC’s platform includes commitments to negotiate more ferry funding from the federal government, and a plan to launch a strategy designed to bring more vessel-production work back to B.C.

“The NDP allowed BC Ferries to send four major shipbuilding contracts and hundreds of jobs to a Chinese state-owned shipyard, strengthening a foreign competitor instead of rebuilding our industrial capacity,” the platform says. “That must never happen again.”

The BC Green Party’s platform also includes a commitment to “build and maintain ships locally” but does not include further details.

Abigail Saxton, a spokesperson for Seaspan, said in an email the shipyard looks forward to working with the federal and provincial governments.

“Seaspan welcomes the recent commitment to the expansion of the province’s shipbuilding infrastructure, supporting not only a made-in-Canada solution, but a made-in-B.C. solution,” Saxton said.
